meta.title: Bullish on Elon: 9 Mega AI Hardware Stocks | NOW
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · Elon's capex thesis, Nvidia, Marvell, Lattice, cooling/power infra, the rest of the field

snapshot: Thesis: Elon Musk will spend "like a drunken sailor" on AI hardware regardless of ROI — SpaceX's own earnings call last week showed 85 cents of every capex dollar going straight into AI hardware.

Base case is 13,000 GB300 server racks already ordered through Foxconn for Macro/Mini Hard (~$52.5B spend); a widely-circulated SemiAnalysis bull case argues for 68,800 racks (~$275-320B), which Kevin partly disputes on internally inconsistent GPU-hour pricing assumptions.

If Elon pushes to a full 10-gigawatt buildout (Reuben-generation racks, ~$4M/rack plus NVLink and Infiniband), total spend could stretch to $400-480B — pushing Nvidia's 2028 revenue estimates up by as much as 50%.
Kevin's declared favorites, in order: Nvidia, Marvell, Lattice Semiconductor — the rest (Vertiv, Eaton, Schneider Electric, Dell, Enphase, ARM) are 'okay' with mixed valuation cases.

Nvidia fair value estimate: $795-850 (PEG 0.76, current PE ~25, forward growth 34%/yr) — called 'dirt freaking cheap' despite being up only 20% YTD and sitting at a $5.4T market cap with 75% gross / 71.4% net margins.

Biggest red flag of the video: Eaton's balance sheet — ~$9.3B+ current debt plus ~$12B long-term debt against only ~$700-800M cash, while still paying dividends and buying back stock at all-time highs.

Not financial advice — Kevin explicitly frames this as "which stocks benefit if Elon overspends," not a call on SpaceX itself (he separately discloses 7-figure SpaceX exposure via his venture fund, bought at a ~$330B valuation, shares not yet delivered due to lockup).

themes.status: BASE CASE 13,000 RACKS ORDERED — BULL CASE UP TO 68,800
themes.title: The Drunken-Sailor Thesis: Elon Will Overspend Regardless of ROI
themes.lead: Kevin's core bet isn't on SpaceX itself — it's that Elon will keep expanding AI hardware supply no matter what the earnings math says, and picks the vendors that get paid either way.
bullets: SpaceX's own earnings call last week showed 85 cents of every capex dollar going straight into AI hardware — the anchor data point for the whole video.
Base case: 13,000 GB300 server racks already ordered through Foxconn for Macro/Mini Hard, ~$52.5B of spend, order already placed.

A SemiAnalysis piece circulating on X argues a bull case of 68,800 rack orders (5.3x the base case) = ~$275-320B of spend; Kevin flags an internal inconsistency in that piece — it prices Elon's GPU-hour revenue at $15-20/hr while pricing Anthropic's cost at only $3/hr in the same article, which he says can't both be true since the LLMs are the ones paying Elon.

If a full 10-gigawatt buildout happens (next-gen Reuben racks, ~$4M/rack plus ~$0.5-1M NVLink plus Infiniband), total spend could stretch to $400-480B, which Kevin says could push Nvidia's 2028 revenue estimates up by as much as 50%.

Google is contractually locked into its SpaceX-adjacent deal and, per Kevin, extremely unlikely to cancel even if Elon delivers late — cancelling would tank SpaceX and force Google to report the fallout in its own earnings.
Memory stocks are deliberately excluded from this list — Kevin says that's a separate video, and these nine picks are outside of memory on purpose.

Personal disclosure up front: Kevin's fund has 7-figure SpaceX exposure bought near a ~$330B valuation (~5x on paper), shares not yet delivered due to lockup; he'd only add more sub-$80/share, which is not a price prediction.

quote.text: None of that freaking crap matters. All that matters is that the richest guy in the world believes it.
quote.cite: — Kevin, on why Elon will overspend regardless of ROI

themes.watch: The entire nine-stock thesis rests on Elon continuing to spend aggressively and on capital markets continuing to fund it via borrowing — Kevin's own framing is that this works 'as long as the stock performs okay, like it stabilizes somewhere,' which is a conditional, not a certainty.

names.name: SpaceX / Elon Musk
names.blurb: The demand driver for the whole thesis; not a stock pick in this video — Kevin explicitly separates 'is Elon overspending good or bad' from 'who benefits if he does.'

names.name: Foxconn
names.blurb: Manufacturing partner receiving the 13,000-rack base-case order; also the entity Wells Fargo flagged as a potential direct-order risk that could bypass Dell (see Dell theme).

themes.title: Nvidia — Biggest Direct Beneficiary, Still Underpriced
themes.lead: Nvidia has a confirmed direct deal with Elon Musk and the best margins in the group, yet Kevin says the market hasn't caught up.
bullets: Confirmed direct deal with Musk; Elon publicly calls Nvidia's chips 'simply the best'; guidance increase expected starting Q4 2026 once the 13,000-rack GB300 order flows through.
Financials: 75% gross margin, 71.4% net margin on $81.6B of revenue — versus 9-28% net margins at most of the other stocks in this list.

Up only 20% YTD despite being the largest direct beneficiary of SpaceX spend — Kevin attributes the gap purely to growth-forecast anxiety, not Twitter/X monetization or SpaceX contract-renewal debates.
Upside math: capturing the full $275-320B SemiAnalysis bull case adds an estimated $100-150B of revenue, ~30% above current 2028 fiscal-year estimates; a full 10GW buildout could push that to +50%.

Vera Rubin ARM-based CPU (paired with Reuben GPUs) is a catalyst Kevin says the market has 'forgotten' — targets Agentic AI orchestration and represents a new ~$20B/year revenue opportunity on its own.

Blackwell inference ramp / NVL72 deployments scaling across hyperscalers are compressing token-generation costs ~60% versus the prior generation, with further compression expected at the Vera Rubin generation.

Red flags: H200-to-China delays (market has largely stopped reacting to China headlines on this stock), heavy reliance on vendor/circular financing, and hyperscalers representing 50% of data-center revenue (a capex-deceleration risk if any of the big four pull back).

quote.text: Nvidia is dirt freaking cheap. None of this is personalized financial advice, but Nvidia is dirt freaking cheap.
quote.cite: — Kevin, closing line of the video

names.name: Nvidia (NVDA)
names.blurb: Fair value $795-850 per Kevin's model (mid-to-high 2s PEG target); current PE ~25, forward growth 34%/yr over 4 years, PEG 0.76. Market cap $5.4T.

themes.title: Marvell and Lattice Semiconductor — The Custom-Silicon Runners-Up
themes.lead: Kevin's second and third favorites both benefit indirectly from Nvidia's own architecture choices rather than from a direct Elon order.
bullets: Marvell (MRVL) makes custom silicon/XPUs (ASICs) for hyperscalers like AWS and Microsoft; Nvidia's new NVLink Fusion architecture lets those XPUs interoperate with Nvidia GPUs and Vera CPUs instead of being locked out — Marvell is one of the first adopters (Google's TPUs have not yet joined), which Kevin frames as a structural advantage.

Relevance to the Elon thesis: Terrafab's D3 chips (orbital) and AI6 chips (FSD/Optimus) are likely custom Tesla-fabricated rather than Marvell parts, but rising NVLink Fusion adoption broadly makes it easier for buyers to keep purchasing Marvell's custom silicon without integration risk.
Long-shot optionality: co-packaged optics (CPOs) and an 'AI RAN' partnership with Nvidia to push inference workloads to 5G/6G base stations — a future call option, not a near-term driver.

Marvell valuation: fair value ~$370 (≈ 69% upside from current), forward growth ~35%/yr, current PEG ~1.43, EPS estimate $4 for Jan 2027, $191B market cap; also has a forecast $10B optics/custom-silicon revenue target if data centers shift from copper toward fiber optics.

Lattice Semiconductor (LSCC) makes FPGAs — 1-2 per server rack historically, expected to rise to 3-4 per rack; every GB300 and Vera Rubin rack carries embedded FPGA content. Server revenue is already 38% of Lattice's total and growing.

Lattice valuation is highly speculative: current PEG just 0.42 (PE ~61) assumes near-doubling of EPS; a slower 40-50% growth scenario implies ~1.5 PEG. High-case fair value $763, low-case $225 — no reliable 4-year estimate exists because the company is too small.

Per-rack economics for Lattice: individual FPGA chips cost $15-50 each, but a single fully-loaded server rack can contain $1,500-5,000 of Lattice hardware and firmware — small unit price, meaningful aggregate exposure.
themes.watch: Lattice's small size means there's no dependable 4-year estimate — Kevin explicitly frames the $225-763 range as high-volatility and speculative, not a tight forecast band.

names.name: Marvell (MRVL)
names.blurb: $191B market cap; strategic Nvidia partnership on custom silicon and optical networking.

names.name: Lattice Semiconductor (LSCC)
names.blurb: ~$18B market cap, ~$130/share; recently acquired a firmware/platform-management company, which is pressuring margins short-term but expected to lift them later.

themes.status: VERTIV = 'NVIDIA PROXY' · EATON = BALANCE-SHEET RED FLAG
themes.title: Cooling and Power Infrastructure: Vertiv vs. Eaton
themes.lead: Both companies get paid regardless of whether SpaceX's own contracts renew, but Kevin's read on their balance sheets is opposite.
bullets: Vertiv (VRT) supplies liquid cooling and chillers — each GB300 rack draws 125kW, about 2.5x an average household's hourly usage, and gets paid on volume regardless of SpaceX contract outcomes. Kevin calls it an 'Nvidia proxy.'

Vertiv fundamentals: operating margin ~18.8-20% and growing, gross margin ~37%, forward EPS estimate $6.68, forward growth ~23-28%/yr. Fair value range $270-390 (28.2% growth assumption); stock already trading near the low end (~$270), so upside is more restrained than the range implies.

Vertiv catalysts: strategic pivot to converged prefabricated power+thermal+IT bundles raises per-site revenue capture and switching costs; incremental service margins run 30-35%; order backlog has stretched to 12-18 month delivery windows; also positioned for the 800V DC power architecture tied to the Vera Rubin generation, plus emerging micro-grid/behind-the-meter energy demand.

Eaton (ETN) also benefits from data-center orders (+85% YoY) and the 800V DC transition, but Kevin flags a serious balance-sheet red flag: current debt (current portion of long-term debt, accounts payable, other current liabilities, accrued comp) has grown to $9.3B+, plus ~$12B of long-term debt, against only ~$700-800M of cash.

Despite the weak liquidity, Eaton is still paying dividends and repurchasing shares at all-time highs — meaning it's financing shareholder returns by borrowing more rather than from free cash. Kevin also flags an elevated short-squeeze risk (four days to cover).

Eaton valuation: EPS $13.46, price ~$448 → PE ~33; forward growth 15.7% → PEG ~2.1 at 17% net margins — 'not much room left' per Kevin, materially less attractive than Vertiv despite similar end-market exposure.

quote.text: The balance sheet strength is absolute trash... the cash is exploded. Like there's no cash. It's gone.

themes.watch: Eaton could still do well purely on order volume from SpaceX-adjacent demand — Kevin's caution is specifically about balance-sheet risk and valuation room, not about the underlying demand story.

names.name: Vertiv (VRT)
names.blurb: ~$100B market cap; smaller analyst coverage than the mega-caps, so estimates (and the valuation range) carry more uncertainty.

names.name: Eaton (ETN)
names.blurb: Data-center orders +85% YoY, but weak balance sheet — Kevin's least-favorite of the 'good demand story' names.

themes.status: SCHNEIDER SKIPPED · DELL AT RISK · ENPHASE AND ARM ARE OPTIONALITY
themes.title: The Rest of the Field: Schneider, Dell, Enphase, ARM
themes.lead: Four names Kevin covers for completeness — one he actively steers away from, one carries a specific disintermediation risk, and two are longer-dated call options rather than near-term plays.
bullets: Schneider Electric (OTC ADR, French company) — data centers are only ~20% of revenue; after adjusting the reported EPS ($11.76) down by 5x for the ADR structure (true EPS $2.35), Kevin gets to ~30x PE, ~14.6% growth, ~2x PEG, 13-14% net margins. His fair value comes out at just $58 — overvalued, and he spends little time on it.

Dell Technologies carries a specific, named risk: Wells Fargo reported SpaceX sending its GB300 server order directly to Foxconn, potentially skipping Dell entirely (not guaranteed). Dell's AI server margins are undisclosed but understood to be mid-single-digit — low margin, high volume.

Dell valuation: trading near a relative high (~$453), implying PE ~24.5x and PEG ~1.26 on ~19.4% growth, but only ~8% net margins. Kevin also discloses a known error in his own valuation tool — its fair-value model assumed only 10% growth versus a more realistic ~19%, meaning the tool's output understates fair value; he flags this transparently as a beta-platform limitation.

Enphase (ENPH) stands out on free cash flow yield — ~7%, far above Nvidia (~2%), Marvell/Palantir-like peers (~1%), Eaton (~2%), Dell (~2%), and Vertiv (~2%). But its data-center angle (IQ solid-state transformers) is a 2028 story still in the RFP stage, and the stock likely won't move until interest rates fall or that product matures — no near-term catalyst.

Enphase valuation: EPS forecast $2 by year-end, stock ~$41-42 → PE ~20.5, growth ~18.6% → PEG ~1.1, net margins 27%. Fair value ~$70-77, framed as a value/optionality play (rate-cut sensitivity plus a 2028 data-center call option), not a current favorite.

ARM licenses CPU cores (not GPUs) — more cores per rack means more ARM revenue, and OpenAI and Meta are already buying its custom silicon (ramping 2027, with AGI CPU revenue expected by fiscal 2031). But related-party revenue tied to China creates volatile, opaque reported income, and its move into hardware manufacturing is a cash-flow drag.

ARM valuation: EPS $2.23 projected for March 2027, price ~$282 → PE ~126x; even at 47.4%/yr forecast growth over 4 years, that's a PEG of ~2.67 — already priced for a lot to go right, which is why Kevin doesn't favor it here.
themes.watch: Kevin's own valuation platform (app.meetkevin.com) is explicitly labeled beta — he discloses one confirmed model error live in the video (Dell's growth assumption), which is a reason to treat any single fair-value number from this source as directional, not precise.

names.blurb: French company; least-favored name in the video on both momentum and valuation grounds.

names.blurb: Foxconn-direct order risk flagged by Wells Fargo; high volume, low margin business model.

names.blurb: Highest free cash flow yield in the group (~7%); 2028 data-center optionality plus rate-cut sensitivity.

names.blurb: CPU-core licensing model; OpenAI and Meta are buying its custom silicon, but valuation already reflects a lot of future growth.

takeaways.title: Kevin's declared ranking is Nvidia, then Marvell, then Lattice Semiconductor — track those three first if following this thesis.
Watch Nvidia's Q4 2026 guidance for confirmation that the 13,000-rack GB300 order is flowing through to revenue as projected.
Treat the 68,800-rack SemiAnalysis bull case skeptically — Kevin himself flags an internal pricing inconsistency in that specific figure.
Before buying Eaton on the data-center-order story, independently check its current balance sheet (debt vs. cash) — the red flag here is specific and quantified, not vague.
Confirm whether Wells Fargo's Dell-disintermediation report (SpaceX ordering direct from Foxconn) firms up in coming quarters before weighting Dell in this thesis.
Enphase and ARM are explicitly framed as longer-dated optionality (2027-2028 catalysts), not near-term momentum plays — size accordingly relative to Nvidia/Marvell/Lattice.

risks: This is a single YouTuber's personal valuation model (app.meetkevin.com), explicitly labeled 'beta' — Kevin discloses one confirmed calculation error live in the video (Dell's growth assumption), so treat every fair-value number here as directional, not audited.

Kevin discloses a material conflict: his venture fund holds 7-figure SpaceX exposure bought near a ~$330B valuation, and he sells access to the valuation platform referenced throughout (course/app members). His stock picks in this video benefit from the same 'Elon overspends' thesis that benefits his own SpaceX position.

All PEG ratios and fair-value targets depend on forward growth estimates that are themselves projections, not reported results — small-cap names in particular (Lattice, Vertiv) are flagged by Kevin himself as having thin or unreliable multi-year analyst coverage.

The transcript is auto-generated from a ~35-minute solo monologue with informal phrasing and occasional crosstalk with a third party at the end — numeric figures (PE/PEG ratios, price targets) have been transcribed as stated but not independently re-verified against company filings.
Kevin explicitly states this is not personalized financial advice and that this video is not a recommendation on SpaceX itself, only on which public-market stocks could benefit if Elon overspends.

other_news.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 teardown aside: bought new for ~$2,500, now reselling ~$4,900 (~2x); roughly 85% of the unit by volume is cooling/frame, not the die itself — used by Kevin to explain why cooling-adjacent stocks (Vertiv, Eaton, Lattice) matter as much as chipmakers.

Someone reportedly put a ~$3.2-3.3M short on SpaceX using only ~$1.5M on a 2x leveraged inverse ETF; Kevin considers this poorly timed, calling the stock's recent low its 'fib bottom' with $133 as the first retracement resistance level.
Kevin's read on Tom Lee's 2027 rally call: Lee 'always thinks there's going to be a rally,' and in Kevin's opinion Lee isn't bullish enough for 2026.

glossary.def: SpaceX/Elon AI-hardware buildout programs referenced as the source of the 13,000 (base case) to 68,800 (bull case) GB300 server-rack orders driving this whole thesis.
Elon/SpaceX-linked chip and hardware program covering orbital (D3) and Optimus/FSD (AI5/AI6) custom silicon, relevant to Marvell's NVLink Fusion optionality.
Custom silicon chips (like Marvell's) built for a specific hyperscaler workload, as opposed to general-purpose Nvidia GPUs.
Nvidia's architecture that lets third-party chips (like Marvell's XPUs) integrate with Nvidia GPUs and Vera CPUs inside the same data center, rather than being excluded.
Price/earnings ratio divided by expected earnings growth rate — used throughout this video instead of plain PE because it accounts for growth; below 1.0 is generally considered cheap.
A reconfigurable chip made by companies like Lattice Semiconductor; used in small quantities (1-4) per server rack for control/management functions.
A power-delivery standard tied to Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin generation; GB300 racks don't require it but can use it, making it a forward-looking positioning point for Vertiv and Eaton.
Free cash flow divided by market cap; used to flag Enphase's ~7% yield as unusually high relative to the other hardware names in this list (mostly ~1-2%).

A US-traded certificate representing shares of a foreign company (here, Schneider Electric); often represents a fraction of one underlying share, which is why Kevin divides Schneider's reported EPS by 5.
